member.summary:
The second most verbose level of logging, debug messages are intended to provide additional information that can be used in debugging or troubleshooting a library or program. This level of message will typically provide information that can be useful to an end user of a library or program.
An should only print messages when it is enabled and its own is set to or .

member.name: F:AVISPL.Logging.LogLevel.Info
member.summary:
Informational messages are intended to provide information to the consumer that is not considered problematic in any manner. Informational messages should not be used for any messages that indicate something went wrong. Use the and messages for logging detailed state and instead use info messages for things such as notices when a module initializes successfully, etc.
An should only print messages when it is enabled and its own is set to , , or .

member.name: F:AVISPL.Logging.LogLevel.Warn
member.summary:
Warning messages are intended to provide information to the consumer about something that could indicate a problem, but isn't an indication of an actual error.
An example of this could be a message about a device that is running low on memory, but hasn't actually run out. Or a non-crucial service that is inaccessible.
An should only print messages when it is enabled and its own is set to , , , or .

member.name: F:AVISPL.Logging.LogLevel.Error
member.summary:
Error messages are intended to provide information to the consumer about any errors that occur that are not considered fatal and will not stop the proper execution of the program.
An example of this could be a message about a service that is required for some aspects of the program to function properly being inaccessible.
An should only print messages when it is enabled and its own is set to , , , , or .

member.name: F:AVISPL.Logging.LogLevel.Fatal
member.summary:
Fatal messages should indicate that something has happened that will cause the originating object, be it a device, a component of a device, a program, etc., to no longer function properly.
An example of this could be a DSP level control printing a message when an attempt is made to control a level that doesn't exist in the DSP project file. Since the component does not exist the corresponding instance will not function at all.
An should always print messages, unless it is entirely disabled.
